productContext: OfficeEMR is a full, all-in-one cloud-based EHR, practice management, and billing suite designed for small and medium-sized ambulatory medical practices. Acquired by EverCommerce (EverHealth division) in 2018. The product integrates clinical charting (customizable templates, progress notes, treatment plans, problem lists, allergies, medications, vitals), e-prescribing (including EPCS and CoverMyMeds integration), scheduling (iScheduler), billing and revenue cycle management (claims submission, clearinghouse integration, eligibility verification, payment posting, electronic statements, fee schedule management), patient portal, telehealth (AnywhereCare), document management (eDocuments/Exydoc/RecordSync), electronic labs and orders, referral management, and public health reporting. Specialty-specific features include nephrology/dialysis rounding, urology, ENT (via ENTChoice/AllMeds integration), orthopedics, neurosurgery, and pain management, with 45+ specialties supported via customizable "Choice EHR" templates. CHPL certification (2022-06-06) covers 37 criteria including (a)(1)-(a)(5) clinical data, (a)(12) family health history, (a)(14) implantable devices, (b)(1)-(b)(3) transitions of care, (b)(10)-(b)(11) EHI export, (e)(1)/(e)(3) patient access, (f)(1)/(f)(2)/(f)(5) public health reporting, (g)(10) FHIR API, and (h)(1) direct messaging. This implies stored data across: demographics, clinical records, prescriptions/e-Rx, lab orders/results, imaging, immunizations, billing/claims/payments, patient portal messages, care plans, referrals, documents, dialysis-specific data, case management, and chronic care management records.

artifacts.summary: 56-page PDF export of the full EHI Export KnowledgeOwl article with all accordion sections expanded. Contains: overview of EHI export purpose and ONC requirements, export settings and role-based access (EHI Export role for single patient, EHI Practice Export role for all patients), step-by-step instructions for both export types, process information for all-patient exports (15-day delivery by Data Export team), naming conventions and file structure documentation, and a complete data dictionary organized into Clinical Data Exports and Practice Management Data Exports sections. The data dictionary lists every export entity with field names and plain-English descriptions. Every field across all 79 entities (excluding readme) has a description.
artifacts.size: 56 pages, covers 79 export entities with 1,051 fields

artifacts.summary: ZIP containing 80 JSON Schema draft-07 files (one per export entity). Each schema defines the array structure (items.properties) with field names and JSON types. All description fields are empty strings — the schemas provide structure/type info only, no semantic descriptions. Two schema files (payment.json, statement.json) have JSON syntax errors (trailing commas). Entity field counts range from 2 (referral_tracking) to 46 (insurance). Total of ~1,013 fields across parseable files.

ZIP containing a single XLSX file (iSalus_EHI_ExportDataElements_published_version1_Oct2023_pristine.xlsx) with two sheets: 'Export File Name Listing' (79 entity names) and 'Export Field Listing' (1,051 rows with columns: Export Name, Field Items, FIELD Position in Export, FIELD, Description, Example, Data Type). All 1,051 fields have descriptions. Provides examples and data types not present in the JSON schemas. This is the most complete field-level documentation artifact.
artifacts.size: 1 XLSX file with 79 entities and 1,051 fields across 2 sheets

artifacts.summary: Complete sample single-patient EHI export for test patient ID 311322. Contains 58 JSON files (57 data entities + readme.json). Each file is a JSON array of record objects. Demonstrates realistic test data: 7 allergies, 134 appointments, 58 claims, 65 claim procedures, 233 lab results, 188 medications, 45 progress notes, 179 template encounters, 18 vitals, 10 immunizations, 4 insurance records, 9 payments, 62 image cross-references, etc. Missing entities (present in schema but absent from sample) include: fee_schedule, sliding_fee, statement, eligibility, hie, immunization_registry, implantable_device, chart_share_detail_*, goal sub-files, health_concern, portal_message — likely because the test patient has no data for those entities.

exportModel.description: The EHI export is a proprietary JSON-based native database dump. Each entity type is exported as a separate JSON file containing an array of record objects. The export covers 79 distinct entities (plus a readme.json with the documentation URL) across clinical and practice management domains. Entities use internal numeric IDs (patientId, claimId, encounterId, etc.) with cross-entity foreign key references (e.g., claimId in claim_procedure linking to claim, encounterId in template_encounter sub-files). The model includes workflow-level objects (orders, claims, prior authorizations, denials, eligibility checks) and specialty-specific entities (dialysis_setup, dialysis_visit, pregnancy, pregnancy_visit, preschool_billing) that would not appear in a standard projection. The single-patient export is self-service via Reports portal; all-patient export requires vendor Data Export team involvement (~15 days). Document images are provided separately in original format (PDF, JPEG, PNG). Per the ehi-export-page.pdf, 'Export Name' files follow a consistent naming convention with .json extension.

While lab results have a dedicated entity, imaging/radiology reports appear to be captured either as progress notes, documents, or within extension encounters rather than having a dedicated structured diagnostic report entity. The data is likely present but distributed across multiple entities.

domainCoverage.gapAnalysis: OfficeEMR offers CCM and RPM services. The export includes case management records, CKCC tracking, chronic care management enrollment data, and remote monitoring status. Coverage is comprehensive.

fieldNamesDocumented.detail: All 79 entities across both the JSON Schema files (80 files, ~1,013 fields with names and types) and the XLSX data dictionary (1,051 fields) include field names. The PDF data dictionary also lists every field name.

fieldTypesDocumented.detail: JSON Schema files provide JSON types (string, number, object, array) for every field. The XLSX includes a 'Data Type' column. Some nullable fields in schemas use 'type: object' incorrectly instead of proper nullable patterns, but types are consistently present.

fieldSemanticsDocumented.detail: The XLSX data dictionary provides plain-English descriptions for all 1,051 fields (100% coverage). The PDF data dictionary mirrors this. In contrast, the JSON Schema files have all description fields as empty strings. The XLSX/PDF descriptions are generally useful (e.g., 'The name of a specific allergen', 'Date and time in UTC when the record was logged, formatted as YYYYMMDDHHMMSS with an offset for Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)').

relationshipsDocumented.detail: Relationships are implicit through shared ID fields (patientId in every entity, claimId in claim_procedure linking to claim, encounterId in template encounter sub-files, goalId in goal sub-entities, authorizationId in prior_authorization sub-entities). The PDF mentions some relationships in passing (e.g., price_estimate_line is '1-to-many' relative to price_estimate). However, there is no formal ERD, no FK documentation, and no explicit join instructions.

valueSetsDocumented.detail: No value set enumerations are documented. Coded fields like claimStatus, gender, maritalStatus, employmentStatus, agingType, progressNoteType, clinicalNoteType, status fields, etc. are typed as strings with no documented allowed values. The XLSX 'Example' column provides some sample values (helping infer formats) but not exhaustive value sets.

sampleDataExists.detail: A complete single-patient sample export (export-311322-voct2023.zip) containing 58 JSON files with realistic test data is provided. It demonstrates actual field values, data formats, and record structures across clinical and billing domains.

documentationQuality.importReadinessRationale: Documentation is reasonably good: all 1,051 fields have names, types, and descriptions via the XLSX/PDF, and a complete sample export demonstrates the format. However, the lack of value set documentation for coded fields, informal relationship documentation (no ERD, no FK specs), inconsistent date formats (YYYYMMDD vs YYYYMMDDHHMMSS-offset), and two malformed schema files (payment.json, statement.json with trailing commas) would require some reverse engineering. A developer could build a functional import with moderate effort but would need to analyze sample data to understand coded values and relationships.

access.notes: All documentation is publicly accessible on KnowledgeOwl knowledge base (no login required). Single-patient export is fully self-service via Reports portal with EHI Export role. All-patient (practice) export requires submission to iSALUS Data Export team with ~15-day delivery, described as being for practices migrating to a new EHR platform. The PDF notes that charges for all-patient exports are 'very limited in scope when the request is for practice moving to a new EHR platform' but does not specify exact fees. Three downloadable artifacts (JSON schemas, XLSX data dictionary, sample export) are directly linked from the main page.

overall.completenessRationale: The export covers 79 entities with 1,051 fields across both clinical and practice management domains, delivered as a native database model in JSON. The product's major data domains — demographics, clinical charting (progress notes + template encounters), medications/e-prescribing, allergies, immunizations, vitals, lab results/orders, problems, care plans/goals, insurance, claims, payments, denials, statements, prior authorizations, documents, patient communications, and specialty-specific data (dialysis, pregnancy, case management) — are all represented with dedicated entities and substantial field counts. The only notable gaps are: (1) no dedicated diagnostic/imaging report entity (likely captured within progress notes or documents), (2) consent is limited to communication preferences rather than clinical consents, (3) telehealth visits lack a dedicated entity (likely captured within progress notes/template encounters), and (4) no fee_schedule entity appears in the sample export despite being referenced in documentation. The export is notably strong on billing/financial data, which is a common gap in other vendors' exports.
overall.postureRationale: This is clearly a comprehensive_native export, not a standard_projection or minimal_or_unclear. The 79-entity JSON export with internal IDs, cross-entity FK references, and workflow-level objects (claims, denials, orders, prior authorizations, eligibility checks) is unmistakably a native database model. The coverage spans both clinical and practice management domains with specialty-specific entities. It falls short of a perfect score primarily because of the lack of value set documentation, the minor gaps noted above, and because we cannot independently verify that no additional internal entities are omitted. It is not partial_native because the coverage is broad with few significant gaps.
overall.strongestSignal: 79 entities with 1,051 fields, all with descriptions in the XLSX data dictionary, covering both clinical and billing/practice management domains including specialty-specific data (dialysis, pregnancy, CKCC). Three complementary artifacts (JSON schemas, XLSX data dictionary, sample export) provide an unusually thorough documentation package for a vendor of this size. (ehi-export-page.pdf, XLSX data dictionary, sample export)
overall.biggestConcern: No value set documentation for coded fields (claimStatus, gender, progressNoteType, etc.) — a consumer cannot interpret many fields without analyzing sample data or reverse engineering. The JSON Schema files have all description fields empty, so the XLSX/PDF is the only source of field semantics. Two schema files (payment.json, statement.json) have JSON syntax errors. (officeemr-b10-schema-v1-oct2023.zip)
overall.narrative:
iSALUS Healthcare's OfficeEMR provides one of the more thorough EHI export implementations seen among smaller EHR vendors. The export is a purpose-built (b)(10) native JSON export covering 79 distinct data entities with 1,051 documented fields, clearly not a repackaged FHIR/C-CDA projection. This is notable because many vendors of similar size simply offer C-CDA exports or minimal data dumps.

The clinical coverage is strong: demographics (41 fields), medications/prescriptions (28 fields with RxNorm, structured sig, NDC), allergies with SNOMED coding, immunizations (30 fields with VIS/VFC tracking), vitals (44 fields with positional BP, pulse ox, glucose), lab results (17 fields with LOINC), problem lists (15 fields with ICD/SNOMED), and comprehensive clinical documentation via both progress notes (with HTML content) and structured template encounters broken into 7 clinical sections.

The billing/financial coverage is particularly strong and uncommon: claims (36 fields with multiple provider roles and three-tier payers), procedure-level claim lines (30 fields with CPT, up to 12 ICD codes), payments (21 fields), denials (11 fields), statements (26 fields with aging buckets), prior authorizations (32 fields), price estimates, sliding fees, and eligibility verification. This contrasts favorably with many vendors who omit billing data entirely from their EHI exports.

Specialty-specific data is also represented: dialysis setup/visits and CKCC tracking for nephrology, pregnancy/prenatal visit data for OB-Gyn, case management records for CCM/RPM programs, and preschool billing.

The documentation quality is good but not exceptional. Three complementary artifacts are provided: JSON Schema files (field names and types, but all descriptions empty), an XLSX data dictionary (all 1,051 fields with descriptions, examples, and data types), and a complete sample single-patient export with 58 JSON files. The main documentation gaps are the absence of value set documentation for coded fields, informal entity relationship documentation (no ERD), and two malformed JSON Schema files.

For a data migration, a developer would have a solid starting point but would need to: analyze sample data to understand coded values, trace relationships through shared IDs, handle inconsistent date formats, and work around the two malformed schema files. The overall package is substantially better than a C-CDA clinical summary export and demonstrates genuine effort to meet the (b)(10) requirement.

notableFacts: 79 entities with 1,051 fields, all with plain-English descriptions in XLSX data dictionary
Native JSON database dump format — not FHIR, C-CDA, or any healthcare standard
Includes both clinical and billing/practice management data (unusual for smaller vendors)
Sample single-patient export with 58 JSON files provided as downloadable artifact
Specialty-specific entities for dialysis (nephrology), pregnancy (OB), and CKCC program tracking
JSON Schema files have all description fields empty — XLSX is the only source of field semantics
Two JSON Schema files (payment.json, statement.json) have syntax errors (trailing commas)
No value set documentation for any coded fields across all entities
Vital signs entity has 44 fields including positional BP (sitting/standing/supine), pulse ox, and body measurements
Single-patient export is self-service; all-patient export requires vendor involvement (~15 days)
